overview: FCG.NZ IS THE CO-OPERATIVE SHARE ITSELF, not the Fonterra Shareholders' Fund — a critically important distinction. FCG.NZ shares are held on the Fonterra Shareholders' Market, a restricted market where ownership and trading are generally limited to current and former supplying farmers, sharemilkers, contract milkers and farm lessors under the co-operative's constitution and Flexible Shareholding rules; an ordinary outside retail or institutional investor most likely CANNOT buy FCG.NZ and would instead need to buy the separate, freely-tradeable Fonterra Shareholders' Fund units (FSF.NZ). FCG shares carry full voting rights (one member, one vote, regardless of shareholding size) and elect the co-operative's board, whereas FSF units carry no vote. Fonterra Co-operative Group is the world's largest dairy exporter, collecting a record 1,571m kgMS of milk in FY2026 (+4.1% YoY, highest in over a decade) from New Zealand farming families and processing it for export to 100+ countries. Following the 31-Mar-2026 completed sale of its global Mainland/Consumer business (Anchor, Mainland, Fernleaf, Western Star, Perfect Italiano, Kapiti) to Lactalis for NZ$4.22bn, Fonterra is now a focused B2B dairy Ingredients and Foodservice exporter; FY2026 (year ended 31 July 2026) delivered Total Group revenue of ~NZ$27bn, reported operating profit of $3.4bn (including a $1.2bn one-off Mainland divestment gain), underlying operating profit of $1.8bn (+23.6% YoY, already exceeding management's original FY28 target to restore pre-divestment earnings), and underlying EPS of 71 cents (up from 54 cents in FY25).

business_model.summary: Fonterra collects NZ farmers' milk and processes it into dairy Ingredients (proteins, milk powders, cheese, casein sold via NZMP/MyNZMP to food manufacturers globally) and Foodservice products (UHT cream, butter, mozzarella, Anchor Food Professionals brand sold to bakeries, QSRs and food service operators, concentrated in Greater China and Southeast Asia). The single largest cost line is the Farmgate Milk Price paid to farmer-suppliers, which is set competitively against a notional efficient processor. Importantly, for FCG.NZ holders specifically (who are, by definition, the same farmers supplying the milk), the Farmgate Milk Price is not simply a cost eroding their investment — it is their principal farm income. A farmer holding FCG shares is paid a high milk price on the milk they supply even when that same high milk price compresses the co-op's reported earnings and share dividend; the two cash flows (milk payment plus dividend) partially offset each other, so the milk-price/earnings tension that is a genuine problem for outside FSF unit holders is much less of a problem — arguably closer to a natural hedge — for the farmer-shareholders who actually hold FCG. Revenue is transactional/commodity-linked rather than recurring/contractual, though a growing 'contracted sales book' and digital channels (MyNZMP, MyNZMP Link) provide some forward revenue visibility. FY2026 total cash distributions to fully shared-up farmer shareholders reached a record $12.42/kgMS ($10.42 total payout plus the $2.00 capital return), underscoring how the co-op funnels earnings back to its farmer-owner base rather than retaining them as a pure corporate.

revenue_streams.name: Ingredients (NZMP proteins, milk powders, cheese, casein, butter/AMF)
Foodservice (Anchor Food Professionals, UHT cream, butter, mozzarella)
Consumer/Mainland Group (Anchor, Mainland, Western Star, Perfect Italiano, Kapiti brands)
revenue_streams.trend: divested 31-Mar-2026 to Lactalis for NZ$4.22bn; no longer part of continuing operations, contributed a one-off $1.2bn divestment gain to FY26 reported operating profit

business_model.customer_type: B2B — global food & beverage manufacturers, foodservice operators, bakeries and QSR chains; virtually no direct B2C exposure post-Mainland divestment
business_model.geographic_mix: Greater China largest single market (Foodservice-led); Southeast Asia (fastest-growing Foodservice region, Vietnam/Indonesia/Thailand); New Zealand (100% of milk collection and manufacturing base, 24 manufacturing sites); Europe, Americas and Rest of AMENA as smaller Ingredients-sales regions; exports to more than 100 countries in total

main_competitors: a2 Milk / Synlait (NZ dairy processors, partly competing for milk supply)
Lactalis (now also a strategic partner/customer post-Mainland sale, and a competing global dairy consumer-brands owner)
US and EU dairy co-operatives/exporters benefiting from rising milk supply
Chinese domestic dairy producers (Yili, Mengniu) reducing China's import reliance
competitive_position.market_position: World's largest dairy exporter, historically responsible for roughly 30% of global cross-border dairy trade; dominant collector of New Zealand's pasture-based milk supply (record 1,571m kgMS in FY26, +4.1% YoY); #1 or top-tier position in global whole milk powder, and a leading position in Foodservice cream/butter/mozzarella supply into Greater China and Southeast Asia

moat_factors.factor: Scale and NZ pasture-based low-cost production
moat_factors.description: NZ's temperate climate enables largely grass-fed, lower-cost milk production versus grain-fed systems elsewhere, and Fonterra's collection/manufacturing network (24 NZ sites) provides scale economics competitors cannot easily replicate domestically

Long-standing relationships with strategic partners (e.g., logistics provider Kotahi) and application/innovation centres in China support reliable delivery into 100+ markets even amid geopolitical disruption
New Zealand Dairy Grass-Fed Administrative Standard and grass-fed data underpin a premium quality/provenance positioning in Ingredients and Foodservice, notably in China and Southeast Asia

Flexible Shareholding requires supplying farmers to hold FCG shares proportional to milk supplied (1-4 shares per kgMS), tying the farmer base's own capital to continued supply and creating switching friction versus rival processors; this is a genuine structural anchor for milk-supply retention, distinct from being a competitive moat over rival processors' products

weaknesses: Fixed NZ milk supply ceiling constrains volume growth; the company competes hard against Open Country Dairy and others just to retain/attract NZ farmer suppliers, though FY26 collections did grow 4.1% to a decade-high 1,571m kgMS
Commodity/cyclical earnings exposed to global milk supply swings (rising US, EU and NZ production drove a mid-2026 cut to the FY2026/27 milk price forecast before a partial recovery by September)

Loss of the higher-margin, brand-differentiated Consumer/Mainland portfolio removes a diversification buffer and a direct-to-consumer brand moat, though FY26 results show the earnings gap already closing faster than the original FY28 target

China import demand has structurally declined as domestic self-sufficiency has grown (Fonterra's own China leadership estimates China will still need to import ~30% of its dairy needs through 2030, but at a lower and more volatile volume than the historical growth trend), reducing the value of Fonterra's largest historical market

Manufacturing cost performance has recently run above strategic targets in prior periods, reflecting NZ input cost inflation and secondary processing costs, even as FY26 capital investment (~$1.035bn, up from $875m in FY25) steps up materially

growth_drivers: Post-Mainland focus on higher-margin, less capital-intensive B2B Ingredients and Foodservice has already delivered underlying operating profit of $1.8bn in FY26 (+23.6% YoY) and underlying ROC of 14.2%, beating both the FY26 10-12% ROC target and the original 'restore FY25 earnings by FY28' timeline
Foodservice expansion beyond Greater China into Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand) leveraging the Anchor Food Professionals brand and grass-fed positioning

Product mix shift toward high-value Advanced & Specialty Ingredients (proteins, functional whey, cheese) — Studholme advanced protein hub reached commercial production in FY26; Clandeboye butter line ($75m), Edendale UHT cream expansion ($150m) and Edgecumbe pastry butter expansion ($35m) all progressing

New incremental ~$1 billion South Island protein manufacturing network investment over three years (operational by 2029, 50-60 permanent jobs), part of a step-up to $1.3-1.6bn annual capex through FY29, including $100-300m/year on cleaner energy/wastewater and ~$600m/year on sustaining capex
Digital sales channels (MyNZMP, MyNZMP Link) improving customer reach/contracted sales visibility and reducing sales friction
Cost discipline and the multi-year ERP transformation targeted to structurally lower cash operating costs per kgMS
Organic milk expansion, capturing a record $14.13/kgMS organic milk price in FY2026

Fresh capital return program (NZ$2.00/share tax-free capital return paid 14-Apr-2026, ~NZ$3.2bn) demonstrates capital discipline; total FY26 cash distributions to fully shared-up farmers reached a record $12.42/kgMS

business.risk: FCG.NZ is a restricted-transfer security most outside investors cannot buy
business.description: FCG shares trade on the Fonterra Shareholders' Market, a market restricted under Fonterra's constitution and Flexible Shareholding rules to current and former supplying farmers, sharemilkers, contract milkers and farm lessors. An ordinary retail or institutional investor is generally not eligible to hold or trade FCG shares at all; anyone reading this analysis as a prospective investment idea should note the practically investable NZX security for outside capital is the separate Fonterra Shareholders' Fund (FSF.NZ), not FCG.NZ. The FCG market is correspondingly thin and illiquid, with a narrow, captive buyer pool of farmer-shareholders rather than the broad market that prices FSF.NZ

China is Fonterra's largest single historical market but its dairy self-sufficiency has risen materially since 2018 (domestic milk production growing ~6%/year), reducing multi-year whole milk powder import volumes; Fonterra's own China leadership expects the country will still need to import roughly 30% of its dairy needs through 2030, but Foodservice growth (UHT cream, butter, mozzarella via bakeries/QSR) is now doing more of the work to offset a structurally slower Ingredients export growth trajectory into China

Divesting Consumer removes a higher-margin, less commodity-linked earnings stream; Fonterra is now more concentrated in commodity-price-sensitive Ingredients earnings — though FY26 results (underlying operating profit +23.6% YoY, ROC of 14.2%) show the earnings recovery arriving well ahead of the original FY28 target

Competing NZ processors (Open Country Dairy, Synlait, Westland) actively compete for farmer milk supply; Fonterra must continually enhance its farmer offering (advance rate flexibility, emissions incentives, shareholding requirement easing) to retain and grow its supplier base, though FY26 collections grew 4.1% to a decade-high

Richard Allen (an 18-year Fonterra veteran, most recently President Global Ingredients) formally became CEO from 1 May 2026, succeeding Miles Hurrell, who stayed on in an advisory capacity through the transition to around September 2026. Allen now owns execution of the ~$1.3-1.6bn/year growth capex programme and the next phase of the post-Mainland strategy without the benefit of Hurrell's multi-year track record

financial.risk: Commodity price cyclicality flowing straight to earnings
financial.description: Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction pricing for whole milk powder and other reference products directly drives both the Farmgate Milk Price (a farmer's income, but the co-op's cost) and Ingredients segment margins; the FY2026/27 milk price forecast was cut from $9.75 to $9.25/kgMS in July 2026 on an 11% GDT fall, then revised back up to a $9.50/kgMS midpoint (range $8.50-$10.50) by September 2026 on improved auction results — illustrating how quickly earnings assumptions can move in both directions within a single quarter. Note that for FCG holders (farmers) the income/dividend impact of a lower milk price is more directly offset by lower farm-gate receipts than for a pure outside investor

financial.risk: Rising capital expenditure and balance sheet capacity
financial.description: FY26 capex stepped up to ~$1.035bn (from $875m in FY25) and management has signalled $1.3-1.6bn/year through FY29, including a new incremental ~$1bn South Island protein investment; net debt was ~$4.9bn at 1H-FY26 (down from $5.5bn) and Fonterra targets Debt-to-EBITDA below 3x and 30-40% gearing, but a sustained multi-year step-up in capex against a cyclical earnings base will need continued discipline to avoid leverage drift
Export-driven revenue is priced predominantly in USD while costs (Farmgate Milk Price, NZ operations) are in NZD; currency movements affect reported margins and the Farmgate Milk Price calculation

Because the buyer pool for FCG shares is restricted to farmers and former farmers, trading volumes and liquidity are structurally lower than a typical NZX-listed equity of comparable size, which can widen bid/ask spreads and increase price volatility around events like the co-operative's capital return

regulatory.description: New Zealand on-farm methane/emissions policy remains a live and evolving area; any future on-farm emissions pricing or compliance cost increases would raise the cost base for Fonterra's supplying farmers and could indirectly pressure the Farmgate Milk Price and Fonterra's own Scope 1-3 targets (net zero by 2050, 2030 interim targets)

As an export-intensive business selling into 100+ countries, Fonterra is exposed to tariff actions, trade agreement changes and geopolitical disruption; China's tariff investigation into EU dairy and broader global trade-war dynamics through 2026 illustrate how quickly dairy trade flows can be reshuffled by policy, even where Fonterra itself is not the direct target. Management has also explicitly flagged Middle East conflict risk to shipping and input costs

Fonterra's Flexible Shareholding rules (minimum/maximum shares per kgMS supplied) and the separate Fonterra Shareholders' Fund cap are periodically revisited by farmer vote; proposals to further restrict the Fund's size and future share-to-unit conversion primarily affect Fund (FSF.NZ) unit holders' float and liquidity — for FCG co-operative shareholders it is arguably neutral-to-mildly-positive, since it retains more of the economic interest in Fonterra within the farmer-owned co-operative rather than leaking it to outside capital

macro.description: Rising milk production from the US, EU and NZ was the primary driver of the mid-2026 Farmgate Milk Price forecast cut; while GDT prices and the FY2026/27 forecast partially recovered by September 2026 (midpoint back up to $9.50/kgMS), a structurally higher global supply environment remains a risk to sustained milk price and Ingredients margins

Adverse weather events can disrupt milk collections for individual farmers even in a record overall-volume season (FY26 collections still grew 4.1% to a decade-high); droughts or extreme weather in future seasons remain a direct volume risk given Fonterra's near-total reliance on NZ pasture-based supply

Long-run growth of plant-based and alternative-protein products is a slow-moving but persistent demand risk for traditional dairy ingredients, particularly in Western retail/consumer categories (less relevant to B2B Ingredients/Foodservice but a latent industry risk)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Underlying global demand for dairy is viewed by management as structurally supported by population growth, a growing global middle class, and consumer trends toward out-of-home dining, healthy ageing and active living, but near-term global supply (US, EU, NZ production growth) has been outpacing demand at times through 2026, driving swings in GDT prices and the Farmgate Milk Price; a partial recovery in GDT auction results by September 2026 lifted the FY2026/27 milk price forecast back toward $9.50/kgMS
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — Fonterra's earnings and the Farmgate Milk Price are both direct functions of global commodity dairy prices (Global Dairy Trade auctions), making the business meaningfully cyclical despite the defensive nature of underlying dairy consumption
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — net debt (~NZ$3.1-4.9bn depending on period) means Fonterra carries meaningful interest expense; a capital-intensive investment programme stepping up to $1.3-1.6bn/year through FY29 also has some rate sensitivity via cost of debt funding
key_input_costs: Farmgate Milk Price (largest single cost, settled at $9.69/kgMS for the 2025/26 season)
Global Dairy Trade reference product pricing (whole milk powder, skim milk powder, protein)

recent_developments.event: Fonterra reported FY2026 (year ended 31 July 2026) annual results: Total Group revenue ~NZ$27bn; reported operating profit $3.4bn (+97.6% YoY, including a $1.2bn one-off Mainland divestment gain); underlying operating profit $1.8bn (+23.6% YoY, up from $1.5bn in FY25); underlying EPS 71 cents (up from 54 cents); underlying ROC 14.2%, well above the 10-12% target range; full-year dividends of 73 cents/share fully imputed (24c interim + 33c final + 16c special Mainland); 2025/26 Farmgate Milk Price settled at $9.69/kgMS, organic milk price a record $14.13/kgMS; total cash distributions to fully shared-up farmers reached $12.42/kgMS ($10.42 payout + $2.00 capital return); FY2026/27 earnings guidance set at 65-85 cents/share and Farmgate Milk Price forecast at $9.50/kgMS (range $8.50-$10.50); management announced an incremental ~$1bn South Island protein manufacturing investment over three years and signalled total capex of $1.3-1.6bn/year through FY29

Fonterra lifted its 2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast midpoint to $9.50/kgMS (range $8.50-$10.50), up from the $9.25/kgMS opening forecast set in July, citing improved GDT auction results for whole milk powder and skim milk powder since the July cut

Richard Allen formally became Fonterra's CEO, succeeding Miles Hurrell; Allen is an 18-year Fonterra veteran who has held roles including VP China Foodservice (Shanghai) and President Americas and Europe (Chicago), most recently serving as President, Global Ingredients

Fonterra cut its opening 2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast to $9.25/kgMS (range $8.00-$10.50), citing an 11% GDT reference-product price fall since May amid strong global milk supply from the US and Europe outpacing demand

Fonterra distributed NZ$3.9 billion in cash to shareholders and unit holders: a tax-free NZ$2.00/share capital return (~$3.2bn, funded by Lactalis sale proceeds) plus a fully imputed 40 cents/share interim distribution (24c ordinary interim dividend, up from 22c, plus a 16c special Mainland dividend representing 100% of Mainland's FY26 earnings while under Fonterra ownership); FSF.NZ's unit price stepped down sharply on the ex-distribution date reflecting the cash paid out, while FCG.NZ (the co-operative share) showed no equivalent step-down — direct market confirmation that FCG and FSF are separate, differently-priced securities despite both referencing Fonterra's underlying performance

Completed sale of Mainland Group (global Consumer and associated businesses: Anchor, Mainland, Fernleaf, Western Star, Perfect Italiano, Kapiti) to Lactalis for NZ$4.22bn, following 98.85% farmer shareholder approval at a 19-Feb-2026 special meeting and satisfaction of regulatory conditions; the transaction generated a $1.2bn one-off gain recognised in FY26 reported operating profit

CEO Miles Hurrell announced his resignation after leading Fonterra since 2018 through the strategic reset and Mainland divestment; he remained in an advisory capacity through the leadership transition to Richard Allen, continuing through around September 2026

H1-FY26 (six months to 31-Jan-2026): Total Group profit after tax $750m (+$21m/+3% YoY), reported EPS 45c; normalised EPS 51c (up 4c YoY excluding $90m of Mainland divestment/separation costs); operating profit up from $1.1bn to $1.2bn on stronger in-market pricing and mix, particularly Foodservice in Southeast Asia and Greater China; net debt reduced from $5.5bn to $4.9bn; return on capital 11.2% (up from 10.4%), tracking within the FY26 10-12% target range; full-year EPS guidance raised to 50-65 cents from 45-65 cents

guidance.management_commentary: Following the Mainland divestment and CEO transition, new CEO Richard Allen (formally in the role from 1 May 2026, an 18-year Fonterra veteran previously President, Global Ingredients) has emphasised that the co-operative reached its earnings-recovery target 'ahead of schedule' and is now investing aggressively (an incremental ~$1bn South Island protein network plus a step-up to $1.3-1.6bn/year total capex through FY29) to convert the leaner post-Mainland business into sustained higher-margin Ingredients and Foodservice growth. Management continues to flag 'significant exposure to changes in commodity prices' given the FY2026/27 sales book is only lightly contracted this early in the season, and has previously cited Middle East conflict risk (shipping, input costs) and rising global milk supply as sources of forecast volatility — illustrated by the FY2026/27 milk price forecast moving from $9.75 (May) to $9.25 (July) to $9.50/kgMS (September) within four months. The Mainland sale has been characterised as 'likely to be the last major asset sale for Fonterra,' with future capital allocation now centred on organic growth investment and continued dividend/capital discipline rather than further portfolio divestment.
guidance.note: Guidance and dividend/capital-return decisions are set by the Fonterra board, which is elected by and accountable to FCG co-operative shareholders (farmers) — i.e., holders of the ticker actually under research here have a direct vote in setting this guidance, unlike Fund (FSF.NZ) unit holders who receive the same per-share cash distributions but have no vote.

fcg_vs_fsf_note.summary: FCG.NZ and FSF.NZ are two separate, independently priced NZX-listed securities that both reference Fonterra Co-operative Group's performance but differ fundamentally in rights and eligible holders.
fcg_vs_fsf_note.fcg_nz: Fonterra Co-operative Group Limited co-operative shares. Held on the restricted Fonterra Shareholders' Market; ownership generally limited to current/former supplying farmers, sharemilkers, contract milkers and farm lessors under Flexible Shareholding rules. Carry full voting rights (elect the board, approve major transactions such as the Mainland divestment and capital return). ~1,609 million shares on issue. Price ~NZ$4.68 (15-Sep-2026).
fcg_vs_fsf_note.fsf_nz: Fonterra Shareholders' Fund units. A separate, open, freely tradeable managed investment scheme available to any investor (retail or institutional), listed on the NZX main board. No voting rights in Fonterra Co-operative Group; investors elect only directors of the Fund's separate corporate Manager. Capped at ~107 million units on issue, with the distribution reinvestment plan currently suspended. Price ~NZ$8.27 (24-Sep-2026, market cap ~NZ$877m).
fcg_vs_fsf_note.why_prices_differ: The persistent price gap (roughly NZ$4.68 for FCG vs NZ$8.27 for FSF, September 2026) reflects genuinely different buyer pools and rights, not measurement error: FSF trades in an open market accessible to all investors and carries a scarcity/liquidity premium plus the option value of eventual governance influence via any future capital-structure change, while FCG trades in a closed, thin market restricted to farmers, for whom the shareholding is bundled with (and partly a precondition of) their milk-supply relationship rather than a pure financial investment. The two prices also diverge visibly around cash events: on the 14-Apr-2026 capital return, FSF stepped down sharply reflecting the cash paid out (its open-market price fully capitalises future distribution rights), while FCG showed no comparable step-down — confirming FCG's restricted farmer market prices the co-operative relationship differently than FSF's open market prices the pure economic security.
fcg_vs_fsf_note.implication_for_this_analysis: Because FCG.NZ is presented here as the researched ticker, this analysis treats it as an operating-company equity analysis of Fonterra Co-operative Group. However, a general investor considering acting on this research should understand they most likely cannot purchase FCG.NZ directly and would need to consider FSF.NZ instead, which carries the same economic (dividend) exposure to Fonterra's results but no vote, a capped/thinning float, and a materially different (higher, and currently policy-uncertain) price.

bull_case: Post-Mainland Fonterra has already delivered on its turnaround thesis: FY2026 underlying operating profit rose 23.6% to $1.8bn and underlying ROC hit 14.2% (well above the 10-12% target), meaning the promised 'return to FY25 earnings by FY28' was achieved roughly two years early

Foodservice growth in Greater China and Southeast Asia (Anchor Food Professionals, UHT cream, butter, mozzarella) continues to outperform, supported by grass-fed provenance branding and an expanding footprint into Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand

FCG shareholders (farmers) hold full voting control of the co-operative and are economically hedged across the milk-price/earnings cycle — a high Farmgate Milk Price directly increases their farm income even when it compresses reported co-op earnings, unlike the position of a pure outside capital provider

Record FY2026 cash distributions to fully shared-up farmers ($12.42/kgMS total, including the $2.00 capital return) plus a 73 cent/share full-year dividend demonstrate the co-op is translating operational improvement directly into farmer/shareholder cash returns under a maintained 60-80% payout policy

A newly announced multi-year investment programme ($1.3-1.6bn/year capex through FY29, including an incremental ~$1bn South Island protein network) targets higher-margin Advanced & Specialty Ingredients and Foodservice capacity, continuing the shift away from commodity milk powder even as FY2027 guidance (65-85c EPS) implies further growth from FY2026's 71c base
bear_case: FCG.NZ is a restricted-transfer security that most outside investors cannot legally hold or trade — it is only tradeable by current/former supplying farmers on the closed Fonterra Shareholders' Market, so this is a largely uninvestable idea for a general investor, who would need to consider the differently-priced, non-voting FSF.NZ units instead

The FCG market is thin and illiquid relative to a typical NZX security of this size, given the narrow, captive farmer buyer pool, which can produce wider spreads and price behaviour that does not always track fundamentals cleanly

China, historically Fonterra's largest market, faces structurally declining import demand for milk powder as domestic self-sufficiency rises (China's own dairy production growing ~6%/year), eroding a multi-decade growth pillar even as Foodservice partially offsets the impact and Fonterra's China team still expects ~30% import reliance through 2030

Earnings remain highly commodity-cyclical: the FY2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast swung from $9.75 (May-2026) to $9.25 (July-2026) back to $9.50/kgMS (September-2026) within four months purely on GDT auction volatility, illustrating how quickly guidance and co-op earnings/dividends can move against holders in either direction (even if the milk-price side of that move is a partial offset for farmer-shareholders specifically)

A materially stepped-up, multi-year capex commitment ($1.3-1.6bn/year through FY29, up from $875m in FY25) is now underway under a still-new CEO (Richard Allen, in role since May 2026) who must execute a large investment programme without yet having a multi-year track record in the top job, at the same time the co-op has lost the diversifying, less-cyclical earnings buffer that the divested Mainland Consumer business used to provide
